text: A hundred waits for a bus, mostly short with a long tail. Textbooks say the average of 30 is safe to treat as a bell. For these waits, does it take 30, 300, or over 1,000? A-B tests lean on that bell's tails. And on revenue data, 30 is off by a factor of thousands. Maybe 30 just means collecting enough waits. Collect 1,000, 10,000, 100,000. The bars get smoother, but the shape doesn't budge. Measure the lean with skewness. The average cubed gap from the mean, left gaps counting negative over the spread cubed. A perfect bell scores zero. These weights for a bus score about two at every sample size. So average instead. Four bus weights. The one long weight gets diluted by three short ones. Drop that one number here. Do that 10,000 times. These averages lean less. skewness 1. 16 per average, 0.5, 64, 0.25, nearly this perfect bell in green. Each time the group grows 4 times, the skewness halves. 2 over root n, and 2 is the skewness of 1 weight. The root comes from the cubes. Add 4 bus weights. Their cubed gaps add up to 4 times 1 weights, but the spread only doubles, so its cube grows 8 times. 4 over 8, half the lean. In general, n over n to the 1.5. Kurtosis, the extra tail weight, fades faster. It quarters each time. Every finer difference fades faster still. Only the bell survives. That's the central limit theorem. It needs independent pieces and one more condition. Back to the textbook's 30. 2 over root 30 0 close to a bell by eye But tests live in the tails A 95 interval should miss 2 on each side Tests estimate the spread from the same data With lopsided weights a low average comes with a small spread, so its interval stops short. With 30 weights, 7% low, 1% high. Ron Kohavi and colleagues want each side between 2 and 3%. Their rule, n at least 355 times the skewness squared. Divide by n and take the root. It's our formula. The average is skewness at most .053. At 300, the lean is .12, still too much. For these weights, 1420, lean .053, and both misses reach the band. Bing's revenue per user had a skewness near 18, 114,000 users, capping each user at $10 a week, under 10,000. And for some data, no number on this axis is enough. A lighthouse one mile off a straight shore flashes at random angles, and each flash lands somewhere on the shore. Track the average landing spot. It never settles. A flash aimed almost along the shore lands absurdly far away and yanks it. Among a thousand flashes, The farthest typically lands about 900 miles off. Divided by a thousand, it still drags the average about a mile. Half of single flashes land within a mile of the middle. Repeat the thousand flash average 200 times, and still only half do. The theorem needs finite variance. No single piece can outweigh the rest. Here the variance is infinite. The median ignores how far the extremes fly, so it homes in. So the answer is over a thousand, not thirty. Collect forever, still lopsided. The bell was never in the data. It's in the average.
